title: Evaluating the socioeconomic impacts of protected areas from rural observatories’ data
text:
1 Using the rural observatory data to assess the protected areas impacts on household living conditions.
This document presents the first steps of an evaluation of the socio-economic impacts of protected areas in Madagascar, based on the Rural Observatory Surveys (ROS) conducted between 1995 and 2015. These longitudinal household surveys offer a rare opportunity to study rural livelihoods over two decades. By linking the ROS to official administrative boundaries and protected area limits, we want to analyze how conservation policies intersect with local livelihoods.
This work combines several methodoligcal approaches to identify impacts of protected areas. The aim is to produce a transparent and reproducible workflow, where each chapter builds the foundations for robust causal analysis, from data cleaning to impact estimation. The provisional results are exploratory, but they already provide insights into the complex and often non-linear relationships between conservation policies and household living conditions.
The document is composed by the following sections:

ROS historical data georeferencing. The available ROS surveys (1995–2015) were not precisely georeferenced and contained variations in place names. We applied a cleaning process and fuzzy matching based on the Common Operational Datasets (CODs) to link each observation to the official communes and fokontany.
Overlaps between ROS data and PAs. Here we analyze the overlap between ROS sites (1995–2015) and the protected areas of the SAPM. Some PAs existed before the surveys, two were created during the survey period, and several after the monitoring ended. This analysis led us to prioritize the Marovoay/Ankarafantsika and Alaotra/Alaotra-CAZ observatory/protected area pairs.
Variable computation calculates and compounds household-level variables from the ROS surveys (1995–2015), covering georeferencing, demographics, education, food security, activities, and income. We systematically address inconsistencies across years—such as changing identifiers, missing modules, and shifts in questionnaire design—while reconstructing comparable indicators at the household level. The result is a consolidated dataset, including partial income measures, that provides a consistent basis for analyzing the impact of protected areas on rural livelihoods over time.
Marovoay-Ankarafantsika section assesses the socio-economic impacts of the 2002 expansion of Ankarafantsika into a national park, combining historical context, spatial mapping of survey sites, and reconstruction of household panels. Treated and control groups were defined across the Betsiboka river and extended to other observatories, and synthetic control methods were applied to income and welfare indicators. At this very preliminary stage, results show no robust positive effects, with agricultural revenues slightly negatively affected and no consistent changes in diversification, food self-sufficiency, or schooling.

title: 2  ROS historical data georeferencing
text:
2.1 Shared geographic reference system
This section provides details about the georeferencing process applied to household panel data collected by the Rural Observatory System (ROS) from 1995 to 2015. The ROS gathered data on various rural contexts in Madagascar. While the data quality was carefully monitored, the survey were not precisely geolocated and, while some fields included mentions to the household place of residence, this were open entry fields and they have not been systematically harmonized or linked to official administrative references. This limits its use in spatially integrated research and public policy evaluation. This appendix aligns the ROS dataset’s various spatial designations with a standardized geographic database, ensuring consistent correlation between each ROS observation and the corresponding geospatial entities, namely communes and fokontany. Similar to other sections of this document, the source code developed to perform all the data processing is accessible by expanding the code blocks, as shown below.
The main purpose of this section is to enhance the georeferencing of the ROS survey data for open data sharing. The initial ROS survey, initiated in 1995, recorded geographical information in varying formats: from “village” to a combination of “municipality”, “village”, and “site”. A significant challenge was that data collection started in 1995, while in Madagascar municipalities were only formally established in 1994, and it took several years required for stabilization. The toponyms, which mostly came from oral traditions, were subjected to change, resulting in varied written representations. Our goal is to identify, disambiguate, and georeference the observations recorded in the ROS data, adopting the Common Operational Datasets (CODs) as a reference, which have been collaboratively defined by OCHA and Madagascar’s BNGRC (National Disaster Management Office).

title: 2  ROS historical data georeferencing
text:
2.1.1 The Common Operational Dataset
CODs are the foundation for all preparedness and response operations, particularly within the humanitarian sector. They were adopted by the IASC in 2008 and revised in 2010, and they play a crucial role in facilitating informed decision-making during the critical initial hours of a crisis. By ensuring consistency among stakeholders, CODs simplify data management and establish a shared operational picture of a crisis. Of particular relevance to our purpose is the inclusion of P-codes in CODs. These unique geographic identification codes can be found in both Administrative Boundary CODs (COD-ABs) and Population Statistics CODs (COD-PSs), and they help overcome challenges posed by variations in place names and spellings. For example, in Madagascar, there are 81 different administrative level 4 (ADM4) features labeled “Morafeno,” with six of them existing within ADM3 features also called “Morafeno.” The only way to distinguish them is through their unique ADM2 features.
P-codes serve as reliable geographic identifiers, eliminating errors that may arise from identical or differently spelled geographic locations. Using the HDX platform, an open platform for cross-crisis data sharing, we retrieve this data to ensure the accurate georeferencing of our ROS data. By leveraging the standardized and official spelling of places provided by P-codes, we can combine, harmonize, and analyze data from various sources, thereby offering a comprehensive and geographically accurate view of the survey’s findings.
Although some level of harmonization is achieved, especially regarding certain variables and household identifiers, the data varies in terms of geographical granularity. In the early years, the data primarily includes a single field indicating the village name. As the years go by, this evolves to include a municipality name, and in later years, an additional “site” name occasionally appears. A comprehensive overview of the observations can be obtained from the “res_deb.dta” files for each year.


2.1.2 Administrative boundaries
The “Madagascar Subnational Administrative Boundaries” dataset is sourced from the Common Operational Datasets (CODs), which provide authoritative reference datasets for decision-making during humanitarian operations. CODs are specifically designed to streamline the discovery and exchange of essential data, ensuring uniformity and using the ‘best available’ datasets. This particular dataset focuses on administrative boundaries, including gazetteers with P-codes, which facilitate organized humanitarian assessments and data management. P-codes act as unique identifiers for every administrative unit and populated area, ensuring standardization in nomenclature. When datasets adhere to the P-code standard, their integration and analysis become more efficient. The dataset provides comprehensive boundary information for Madagascar at five administrative levels: country, region, district, commune, and fokontany. It is accessible for download as shapefiles from the provided link.


2.1.3 Localities
The “Madagascar Populated Places” dataset is also part of the Common Operational Datasets (CODs). This dataset includes populated place points for Madagascar. The data has been sourced from the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency and provided by the University of Georgia - ITOS. Furthermore, the Geographic Information Support Team (GIST) has taken on the role of distributor, with the data being published on 2007-03-07. UN OCHA ROSA has enhanced the dataset by adding P-codes and administrative boundary names based on the BNGRC (National Disaster Management Office) data. The dataset geolocates 28,184 populated places with their toponyms (names), codes related to various administrative levels such as fokontany, commune, district, and region, as well as their spatial coordinates.


Code
# Load datasets
ROS_surveys_2007 <- read_dta(paste0(ros_data_loc, "2007/res_deb.dta"))
observatory_names <- read_xlsx("data/observatory_names.xlsx")

obs_communes <- st_read(
  "data/Observatoires_ROS_communes_COD_v4.gpkg",
  quiet = TRUE) 
pop_places <- st_read(
  "data/OCHA_BNGRC populated places/mdg_pplp_places_NGA_OCHA.shp", quiet = TRUE)

title: 2  ROS historical data georeferencing
text:
2.2 Georeferencing methodology

2.2.1 Simplify strings
The treatment of toponyms presents a unique challenge, especially when these names are captured from varied sources. In the dataset, these names can vary due to differences in languages, case sensitivity, and the inclusion of additional descriptive terms. To address this, the clean_string function was developed. This function begins by converting all strings to lowercase, ensuring that subsequent comparisons are not sensitive to case variations. Next, to create a uniform standard, all non-alphanumeric characters are removed, retaining only spaces and the alphanumeric content. Common qualifiers in toponyms, such as “centre”, “haut” (high) or “bas” (low), which are not consistently used across records, are also removed. Given the bilingual nature of the dataset, with entries potentially in both Malagasy and French, the function translates cardinal points to the Malagasy language to ensure uniformity. Lastly, certain locales with multiple names, such as “Fort Dauphin”, also known as “Taolagnaro”, “Tolagnaro” or “Tolanaro”, are standardized to a single term, “Tolanaro”, to eliminate potential disparities. We also address instances of Roman numerals from I to VI, converting them to their Arabic numeral counterparts, ensuring consistent representation across records.


Code
clean_string <- function(x){
  x %>%
    tolower() %>% # Convert to lowercase
    # Retain spaces, remove other non-alphanumeric characters
    str_replace_all("[^[:alnum:][:space:]]", " ") %>% 
    str_remove_all("\\b(centre|haut|bas|androy)\\b") %>%
    str_trim() %>% # Trim spaces from start and end of string
    str_replace_all("\\bcentre\\b", "") %>% # Remove the word 'centre'
    # Translate cardinal points
    str_replace_all("\\bnord\\b", "avaratra") %>% 
    str_replace_all("\\best\\b", "atsinanana") %>%
    str_replace_all("\\bouest\\b", "andrefana") %>% 
    str_replace_all("\\bsud\\b", "atsimo") %>% 
    str_replace_all("\\batsinana\\b", "atsinanana") %>% # Replace short form 
    str_replace_all("(fort dauphin)|(taolagnaro)|(tolagnaro)", 
                    "tolanaro") %>% # Variations for fort dauphin
    # Convert Roman numerals to Arabic
    str_replace_all("\\bi\\b", "1") %>% 
    str_replace_all("\\bii\\b", "2") %>%
    str_replace_all("\\biii\\b", "3") %>% 
    str_replace_all("\\biv\\b", "4") %>% 
    str_replace_all("\\bv\\b", "5") %>% 
    str_replace_all("\\bvi\\b", "6")
}




2.2.2 Fuzzy matching
By default, statistical softwares and computing languages match text by pairing only identical strings. Exact string matching is inappropriate in our context, where location data entry was subject to human errors like typographical mistakes or minor variations in spelling. To avoid this rigidity, fuzzy matching is employed. This approach gauges the degree of similarity between two strings, bypassing the need for an exact character-to-character match. The principle metric adopted for this is the “Levenshtein distance,” which quantifies the minimum number of single-character edits required to change one string into another. The fuzzy_match function encapsulates this approach. The function initiates the process by filtering the reference list of encontered toponyms based on a given observatory code, which considerably narrows down potential matches. Then, using the Jaro-Winkler distance metric — a variant of the Levenshtein distance particularly suited for shorter strings — the function computes the similarity between the target string and entries in the filtered reference. To ensure that only relevant matches are acknowledged, a threshold, termed max_distance, is set. Matches that exceed this threshold are disregarded. For those that pass this validation, the function then extracts the pertinent details of the matched row from the reference dataframe.


Code
fuzzy_match <- function(target_string, dataframe, column_name, observatory_code, 
                        max_distance = 0.25) {
  # Filter the dataframe based on observatory_code
  filtered_reference <- dataframe %>%
    filter(OBS_CODE == observatory_code) %>%
    select(all_of(column_name), ADM3_PCODE, ADM3_EN)
  
  # If filtered_reference is empty, return NA values
  if (nrow(filtered_reference) == 0) {
    return(list(matched_string = NA, ADM3_PCODE = NA, ADM3_EN = NA, distance = 1))
  }
  
  # Use stringdist to find the closest match
  distances <- stringdist::stringdistmatrix(target_string, filtered_reference[[column_name]], method = "jw")
  
  # If there are no valid distances, set min_distance to Inf
  if(all(is.na(distances))) {
    min_distance <- Inf
  } else {
    min_distance <- min(distances, na.rm = TRUE)  # Ensure NA values don't affect the min calculation
  }
  
  # Check for Inf distance and replace it with 1
  if (is.infinite(min_distance)) {
    min_distance <- 1
  }
  
  # If min_distance exceeds the max_distance threshold, return NA values
  if (min_distance > max_distance) {
    return(list(matched_string = NA, ADM3_PCODE = NA, ADM3_EN = NA, distance = NA))
  }
  
  matched_row <- filtered_reference[which.min(distances), ]
  
  return(list(matched_string = matched_row[[column_name]], 
              ADM3_PCODE = matched_row$ADM3_PCODE, 
              ADM3_EN = matched_row$ADM3_EN, 
              distance = min_distance))
}




2.2.3 Hierarchical matching of data
The hierarchical organization of spatial entities is key for our challenge. Such an organization allows for a cascading representation of data, starting from broader scopes and narrowing down to more specific layers. This representation is reminiscent of the defining order of geographical entities: regions contain provinces, which contain municipalities, and these in turn contain localities. In the georeferencing context, leveraging this hierarchical structure can lead to more precise matches. For instance, if an observatory code is associated with a specific district, the search for matches is confined to that district, enhancing both the efficiency and accuracy of the process. ?fig-spatial-hierarchies represents this hierarchical arrangement, serving as a roadmap for the subsequent data matching tasks.

Madagascar’s current administrative setup is straightforward: regions contain districts; districts have communes; and communes are made up of Fokontany. Though a Fokontany should in principle be a single village, it often includes multiple villages or populated areas. It’s worth noting that while the idea of communes has been around for a while, they were only officially recognized in 1994. However, rolling them out took some time after 1994. Before 1994, “communes” simply described local government areas without any formal administrative status. The regions were created in 2004. On the ROS side, observatory referred during the first surveys to villages. A systematic registry of the communes only started in the 2004 and 2005 rounds, depending on the observatories. A mention to “sites” also appeared in 2011 but was scarcely documented. Our strategy was to established links between the village information and populated places, and between communes.

title: 2  ROS historical data georeferencing
text:
2.3 A Detailed walk-through
We now break down our approach to describe each subsequent step. We began by exploring the ROS documentation, and in particular the reports associated to community survey, that contain descriptions of the area surveyed by each observatory. While doing so, we updated the COD subnational administrative boundary dataset by adding a field named OBS_Y_N. This field was marked as ‘1’ if the municipality was listed in an observatory survey; if not, it was left empty. Additionally, we added another field, OBS_NUM, which would store the observatory number. If the municipality wasn’t part of any survey, this field was left empty. The list of observatories and surveyed municipalities can be found in the Table 2.2.
Next, we moved on to geolocation, which took place in four stages. Each stage depended heavily on the data quality and completeness obtained from the previous ones.

2.3.1 Method 1 : Fuzzy matching from registered municipality names
This phase involved a systematic alignment process for the municipalities. When municipality names were included in our dataset, we attempted to correlate them with names of municipalities identified as data collection locations. To ensure accuracy, this alignment was carried out separately for each observatory. Due to possible differences in terminology across sources, a fuzzy matching algorithm was used. This method calculates the likelihood of two different names referring to the same entity. Once a probable match was identified, we visually verified all matches and flagged any false positives for removal.
The following code segment details the methodology applied:


Code
# List of years
years <- 1995:2015

# Read all datasets and combine
all_surveys_description <- map_df(years, function(year) {
  df <- read_dta(paste0(ros_data_loc, year, "/res_deb.dta"))
    # Convert all columns to character to ensure consistency
  df <- df %>% mutate_all(as.character)
  return(df)
})

# Extract unique combinations and list all the years they appeared in
unique_combinations <- all_surveys_description %>%
  group_by(j0, j42, j4) %>%
  summarize(years = toString(unique(year)),
            obs_count = n()) %>%
  ungroup()

# Harmonize the fields that contain municipality or village names
unique_combinations <- unique_combinations %>%
  mutate(clean_muni = clean_string(j42),
         clean_village = clean_string(j4))
obs_communes <- obs_communes %>%
  mutate(clean_ADM3 = clean_string(ADM3_EN))
pop_places <- pop_places %>%
  mutate(clean_pname = clean_string(PLACE_NAME)) 

# List of observatories for which municipalities have been identified
identified_observatories <- unique(obs_communes$OBS_CODE) %>%
  na.omit()
# Filter for the observatory for which we already have a manual identification
# of municipalities
unique_combinations <- unique_combinations %>%
  filter(j0 %in% identified_observatories) 

# Apply the fuzzy matching observatory-wise
results <- map2_df(unique_combinations$clean_muni, 
                   unique_combinations$j0, 
                   ~ as.data.frame(t(
                     fuzzy_match(.x, obs_communes, "clean_ADM3", .y))))  %>%
  unnest(cols = c(matched_string, distance, ADM3_PCODE, ADM3_EN))

# Combine the results with the unique_combinations
correspondence_table <- bind_cols(unique_combinations, results) 

# Add a column for the matching method
correspondence_table <- correspondence_table %>%
  mutate(method = ifelse(!is.na(matched_string), "method_1", NA_character_))


To synthesize and visually represent our matches, the identified municipalities are plotted on a map:


Code
# Extract matched resuts
matched_results <- unique(correspondence_table$ADM3_PCODE) %>%
  na.omit()
# Keep municipalities in those
matched_spatial <- obs_communes %>%
  filter(ADM3_PCODE %in% matched_results)

tmap_mode("view")
# Plot
tm_shape(matched_spatial) +
  tm_polygons(col = "OBS_NAME")




2.3.2 Method 2: Extracting municipality names from text in “village names”
For observations where the field “municipality name” was empty (all cases before 2004 and still a frequent situation afterwards), we turned our attention to the village name field. The objective was to determine whether these village names could potentially contain a municipality’s name that had been previously identified during the observatory surveys. For the observations with no municipality value, we extracted the first word or segment in the village name. This extracted word then underwent a process of fuzzy matching against the list of identified municipalities’ names. However, manual verification identified errors. Certain matches, which we labeled as ‘false positives’, were found to be errors and were removed from the results. Once this cleansing step was completed, we included the validated matches back into the primary correspondence table.


Code
# Filter out matched municipalities and extract the first word
unmatched_results <- correspondence_table %>%
  filter(is.na(matched_string)) %>%
  select(j0:clean_village) %>%
  mutate(first_word = str_extract(clean_village, "^[^\\s/]+"))

# Fuzzy matching with the first word and identified municipalities
results_step2 <- map2_df(unmatched_results$first_word, 
                         unmatched_results$j0, 
                         ~ as.data.frame(t(
                           fuzzy_match(.x, obs_communes, "clean_ADM3", .y))))  %>%
  unnest(cols = c(matched_string, distance, ADM3_PCODE, ADM3_EN))

# Update Results
potential_matches2 <- bind_cols(unmatched_results, results_step2)

# Manually identify false positives and remove them
false_positives <- c("madiromionga", "maroarla", "tsaratanteraka", 
                    "ambatoharanana", "ambatoaranana", "maroala", "erakoja", 
                    "erakoka", "maroalo", "erakka", "erakoa")
validated_matches2 <- potential_matches2 %>%
  mutate(across(c(matched_string, ADM3_PCODE, ADM3_EN, distance),
               ~ ifelse(first_word %in% false_positives, NA, .)),
         method = ifelse(!is.na(matched_string), "method_2", NA_character_))

# Integrate new results in correspondence table
correspondence_table <- correspondence_table %>%
  filter(!is.na(matched_string)) %>%
  bind_rows(validated_matches2) %>%
  select(-first_word)




2.3.3 Method 3: Village name fuzzy matching with populated places
With some observations still devoid of a matched municipality, we initiated another processing layer. This phase saw the unmatched village names being subjected to fuzzy matching against the populated places dataset described above. We first sifted out the unmatched results from our prior analysis. Then, we augmented the ‘pop_places’ dataset with observatory codes for the entries that were located in communes recognized as surveyed by observatories. Next we performed another fuzzy matching, comparing the village names against the ‘pop_places’ names. To maintain a level of precision, we set a restrictive threshold, dismissing any match that exceeded a certain “distance” or degree of difference. But, as with the previous methods, visual verification revealed some mismatches. These ‘false positives’ were flagged and discarded and the remaining ones were integrated into the overarching correspondence table.


Code
# Re-filter unmatched results
unmatched_results2 <- correspondence_table %>%
  filter(is.na(matched_string)) %>%
  select(j0:clean_village)

# Join OBS_CODE to pop_places
pop_places <- pop_places %>%
  rename(ADM3_PCODE = COM_PCODE, ADM3_EN = COMMUNE) %>%
  mutate(ADM3_PCODE = str_replace(ADM3_PCODE, "^MDG", "MG")) %>%
  left_join(select(obs_communes, ADM3_PCODE, OBS_CODE) %>%
                     st_drop_geometry(), 
            by = "ADM3_PCODE")

# Apply the fuzzy matching observatory-wise
results_step3 <- map2_df(unmatched_results2$clean_village, 
                         unmatched_results2$j0, 
                         ~ as.data.frame(t(
                           fuzzy_match(.x, pop_places, "clean_pname", .y,
                                       max_distance = 0.22))))  %>% # erratic results beyond
  unnest(cols = c(matched_string, distance, ADM3_PCODE, ADM3_EN))

# Bind the results with unmatched_results_v2
potential_matches3 <- bind_cols(unmatched_results2, results_step3)

# Manually identify false positives and remove them
false_positives2 <- c("analambarika", "maroaloka", "ambakela", "ambodirofia",
                      "ambohibao", "ambato mangabe", "marofonaritra", 
                      "andranovo ambodimanga", "morataitra", "antanambao", 
                      "ankililoa")
validated_matches3 <- potential_matches3 %>%
  mutate(across(c(matched_string, ADM3_PCODE, ADM3_EN, distance),
               ~ ifelse(clean_village %in% false_positives2, NA, .)),
         method = ifelse(!is.na(matched_string), "method_3", NA_character_))

correspondence_table <- correspondence_table %>%
  filter(!is.na(matched_string)) %>%
  bind_rows(validated_matches3)




2.3.4 Method 4
For the remaining, we try matching with other village names for which the municipality has been matched.
Even after the above measures, there remained observations that had eluded a municipality match. The subsequent strategy was to juxtapose them with other village names that had already been successfully matched to a municipality. We assembled a table comprising municipality names and their paired village names, using data from previous successful matches. Then the still-unmatched village names were run through a fuzzy matching process against the known village names. We fine-tuned the algorithm with a restrictive matching threshold. Again, some matches stood out as anomalies. Labeled as ‘false positives’, these were sifted out and the newly matched data was incorporated into the main correspondence table.


Code
# Create a list of municipality names and village names for matched observations
matched_villages <- correspondence_table %>%
  filter(!is.na(method)) %>%
  select(j0, ADM3_PCODE, ADM3_EN, clean_village) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  rename(OBS_CODE = j0)

# Re-filter unmatched results
unmatched_results3 <- correspondence_table %>%
  filter(is.na(method)) %>%
  select(j0:clean_village)

# Try matching unmatched villages against matched village names observatory-wise
results_village_match <- map2_df(
  unmatched_results3$clean_village, unmatched_results3$j0,
  ~ as.data.frame(t(fuzzy_match(.x, matched_villages, "clean_village",
                                .y, max_distance = 0.28)))) %>%
  unnest(cols = c(matched_string, distance, ADM3_PCODE, ADM3_EN))
# Bind these results with unmatched_results_v3
potential_matches4 <- bind_cols(unmatched_results3, results_village_match)

# Manually identify false positives and remove them
false_positives4 <- c("amp0mbibitika antanakova", "arakoke ambonano ampihamibe", 
                      "farara farara", "farara ambakela", "fara ambakela", 
                      "ambatotelo marofinaritra")
validated_matches4 <- potential_matches4 %>%
  mutate(across(c(matched_string, ADM3_PCODE, ADM3_EN, distance),
               ~ ifelse(clean_village %in% false_positives4, NA, .)),
         method = ifelse(!is.na(matched_string), "method_4", NA_character_))


# Merge the updated results back to the correspondence table
correspondence_table <- correspondence_table %>%
  filter(!is.na(matched_string)) %>%
  bind_rows(validated_matches4)

title: 2  ROS historical data georeferencing
text:
2.4 Matching villages
After successfully matching commune names with an official, normalized reference, our next goal is to align the villages as identified by the ROS with their administrative counterpart, known as Fokontany. This task presents challenges, notably because the ROS village identifications weren’t directly linked to Fokontany names, and the Fokontany names themselves have undergone changes. Additionally, variations in village naming within the ROS dataset complicate the process. Our approach involves several steps: First, we load the official COD Fokontany dataset. Next, we standardize the place names using our previously discussed clean_string function. Then, using the purpose-built fuzzy_match_village function, we assess the similarity between the village names in the ROS dataset and the Fokontany names within the same commune, specifically by calculating the Jaro-Winkler distance between the strings(see ?sec-anonymization for more details on the Jaro-Winkler distance). We select the names with the highest degree of matching. During a manual review of these results, we closely examined the matches, especially those with larger Jaro-Winkler distance. From this examination, we derived a distance of 0.2, below which the majority of matches were accurate. Notably, some matches above this threshold were deemed accurate and retained, while a small number of matches below this threshold were identified as false positives and subsequently discarded.


Code
# Load the ADM4 dataset, which corresponds to Fokontany
fokontany <- st_read("data/OCHA_BNGRC admin boundaries/mdg_admbnda_adm4_BNGRC_OCHA_20181031.shp",
                      quiet = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(ADM4_clean = clean_string(ADM4_EN))

# A function to perform fuzzy matching with Fokontany or populated places
fuzzy_match_village <- function(target_string, dataframe, column_name, 
                                ADM3_PCODE_filter, id_column, 
                                municipality_string = NULL, max_distance = 0.4) {
  
  # Check if target_string has multiple words and if the first word matches the municipality_string
  if (!is.null(municipality_string) && length(unlist(strsplit(target_string, " "))) > 1) {
    first_word <- unlist(strsplit(target_string, " "))[1]
    distances_municipality <- stringdist::stringdist(first_word, municipality_string, method = "jw")
    if (min(distances_municipality, na.rm = TRUE) <= max_distance) {
      target_string <- str_remove(target_string, paste0("^", first_word, " "))
    }
  }
  
  filtered_reference <- dataframe %>%
                          filter(ADM3_PCODE == ADM3_PCODE_filter) %>%
                          select(all_of(column_name), all_of(id_column))
  
  # If filtered_reference is empty, return NA values
  if (nrow(filtered_reference) == 0) {
    return(list(matched_string = NA, ID = NA, geometry = NA, distance = 1))
  }
  
  # Use stringdist to find the closest match
  distances <- stringdist::stringdistmatrix(
    target_string, filtered_reference[[column_name]], method = "jw")
  
  # If there are no valid distances, set min_distance to Inf
  if(all(is.na(distances))) {
    min_distance <- Inf
  } else {
    min_distance <- min(distances, na.rm = TRUE)
  }
  
  # Check for Inf distance and replace it with 1
  if (is.infinite(min_distance)) {
    min_distance <- 1
  }
  
  # If min_distance exceeds the max_distance threshold, return NA values
  if (min_distance > max_distance) {
    return(list(matched_string = NA, ID = NA, geometry = NA, 
                distance = NA))
  }
  
  matched_row <- filtered_reference[which.min(distances), ]
  
  return(list(matched_string = matched_row[[column_name]], 
              ID = matched_row[[id_column]], 
              distance = min_distance))
}

2.5 Validating the Quality of Georeferenced Data
To ensure the robustness and validity of our georeferenced data, we employ a multi-tiered validation approach that hinges on quantitative metrics and qualitative consistency checks.

2.5.1 Quantitative metrics
We first look at the distribution of the unique observations that were successfully matched during the various stages of the georeferencing process.



Table 2.1: Number of ROS observation which commune and village were matched



Code
# Re-format modality labels  
matching_tbl <- correspondence_table3 %>%
  mutate(method = case_when(
    method == "method_1" ~ "Method 1",
    method == "method_2" ~ "Method 2",
    method == "method_3" ~ "Method 3",
    method == "method_4" ~ "Method 4",
    is.na(method) ~ "Unmatched communes"),
    method_village = case_when(
      method_village == "method_5" ~ "Matched villages",
      is.na(method_village) ~ "Unmatched villages"))

summarized_data <- matching_tbl %>%
  group_by(method, method_village) %>%
  summarize(total_obs = sum(obs_count, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(percent_obs = total_obs/sum(total_obs))

count_tbl <- summarized_data %>%
  select(method, method_village, total_obs) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = method_village, values_from = total_obs, 
              values_fill = 0) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(Total = sum(c(`Matched villages`, `Unmatched villages`))) %>%
  ungroup()  %>%
  adorn_totals("row")

percent_tbl <- summarized_data %>%
  select(method, method_village, percent_obs) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = method_village, values_from = percent_obs, 
              values_fill = 0) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(`Total (%)` = sum(c(`Matched villages`, `Unmatched villages`))) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename(`Matched villages (%)` = `Matched villages`,
         `Unmatched villages (%)` = `Unmatched villages`) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x * 100, 2)),
         across(where(is.numeric))) %>%
  adorn_totals("row")


summarized_data2 <- count_tbl %>%
  left_join(percent_tbl, by = "method") %>%
  relocate(method, `Matched villages`, `Matched villages (%)`, 
           `Unmatched villages`, `Unmatched villages (%)`,
           Total, `Total (%)`) %>%
  rename(`Commune matching method` = method)

gt(summarized_data2)  %>%
  # Add a title
  tab_header(title = "Result of matching process",
             subtitle = "Number of survey observation per method")

title: 2  ROS historical data georeferencing
text:
2.6 Conclusion
Given the variability in location labels recorded in the ROS data, we emphasized standardizing and aligning toponyms. We introduced the clean_string function to unify place names, addressing variances in language, letter casing, and o ther descriptors. Utilizing fuzzy matching, we connected similar text strings, using the Levenshtein distance as a benchmark. To heighten accuracy, a hierarchical data matching strategy was applied, reflecting the inherent structure of geographical units, where regions envelop districts, which further consist of municipalities and localities. The COD data, curated by BNGRC and OCHA, was our reference point for these matches. Various techniques, including hierarchical fuzzy matching and visual checks, were employed.
As a result, we could automatically match 98% of commune name variations in the dataset with an official commune, and 62% of village name variations with a fokontany. The outcomes are consistent with ROS’s internal documentation, and the spatial representations can be further inspected for validation. Future corrections and enhancements are anticipated, and our system, leveraging Quarto notebook and reproducible R code, will facilitate these refinements.
ROS began its data collection at a time when geolocation best practices weren’t as evolved as they are today. Should more survey rounds be conducted in the future, the intricate georeferencing process demonstrated here should serve both as a cautionary tale and a guide on optimizing data registration (for instance, using PCODES). We’re optimistic that refining the georeferencing of past ROS data, as presented in this work, will amplify the data’s utility for both research and policy decisions.

3.2 Inventory of ROS data
Before analyzing overlaps with PAs, we establish a complete inventory of the ROS survey data. We load the household-level datasets for each year between 1995 and 2015 and count the number of households surveyed per observatory. This provides the temporal coverage required to assess potential baselines and follow-up data.

# Select appropriate folder as data source
data_path <- "data/ROS_MDG_microdata/"

# Define a function to load and count surveys per observatory for a given year
load_and_count <- function(year, factorize = FALSE) {
  # Define file path
  file_path <- paste0(data_path, year, "/res_deb.dta")
  
  # Load data
  data <- read_dta(file_path)
  
  # Extract label and convert to factors if option
  if (factorize) {
    data <- data %>%
      mutate(across(everything(), as.character),
             across(where(is.labelled), ~ as.character(as_factor(.))))
  }
  
  # Count surveys per observatory
  count_data <- data %>%
    group_by(j0) %>%
    summarise(survey_count = n()) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    mutate(year = year)  # Add year column
  
  return(count_data)
}

3.7 Limitations and next steps
It is important to note that ROS observatories represent a unique opportunity to obtain long time baseline and follow-up data on socioeconomic impacts of PAs, but ROS were not designed with conservation impacts in mind. Their locations were chosen for agricultural and socio-economic monitoring, not proximity to PAs. As such, overlaps are partly coincidental and require cautious interpretation.

title: 4  Variable computation
text:
4.1 Georeferencing households
In this chapter we build a harmonized dataset of household-level variables across all ROS survey years (1995–2015). This involves three steps: (i) georeferencing households, (ii) constructing demographic, educational, and food security indicators, and (iii) reconstructing income variables. Each step requires dealing with inconsistencies across years in the structure of the questionnaires and the naming of variables.
We begin by linking household identifiers (j5) with locality codes and administrative boundaries. Because the format of identifiers changed in early survey years, we implement corrections using the 1996 survey as a reference to align identifiers from 1995.
Code
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(haven)
library(readxl)
library(labelled)


# Load the locality correspondence table with administrative codes
locality_reference <- readr::read_rds("output/correspondence_table5.rds") %>% 
  select(j0, j42, j4, ADM3_PCODE, ADM3_EN, ADM4_PCODE, ADM4_clean)

# Load observatory names and match them to their codes
observatory_labels <- read_xlsx("data/observatory_names.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(code = as.character(code)) %>%
  select(code, name)

# Function to rename variables using a named list
# e.g. renames = list("j0" = c("obsr", "obsr96"))
rename_all_custom <- function(df, renames) {
  if (length(renames) == 0) return(df)
  for (new_name in names(renames)) {
    # Skip renaming if new_name already exists in df
    if (new_name %in% names(df)) next
    old_names <- renames[[new_name]]
    matched_old <- old_names[old_names %in% names(df)]
    if (length(matched_old) > 0) {
      df <- df %>% rename(!!new_name := all_of(matched_old[1]))
    }
  }
  return(df)
}

# Generic function to load and standardize records from any year
# Arguments:
#   - year: numeric year of the survey
#   - vars: vector of variables to select (after renaming)
#   - renames: named list of renaming rules (new_name = c(possible_old_names))
load_records <- function(year, file_name, vars, renames = list()) {
  path <- paste0("data/ROS_MDG_microdata/", year, "/")
  df <- read_dta(paste0(path, file_name))

  df <- rename_all_custom(df, renames)

  # Ensure all expected vars exist (fill missing with NA)
  missing_vars <- setdiff(vars, names(df))
  df[missing_vars] <- NA

  # Handle j0 if not in original file
  if (!"j0" %in% names(df)) {
    df <- df %>%
      mutate(j0 = substr(j5, 1, 2)) %>% 
      mutate(j0 = as.character(as.numeric(j0)))
  }

  df %>%
    mutate(j0 = as.character(as.numeric(j0))) %>%
    select(any_of(vars))
}

# Define variables to extract from res_deb files
vars_res_deb <- c("year", "j0", "j5", "j4", "j42")
renames_res_deb <- list("j0" = c("obsr", "obsr96"))
# Load res_deb for all years using the same generic function
household_locality_all <- map_dfr(
  1995:2015,
  ~load_records(.x, file_name = "res_deb.dta", vars = vars_res_deb, 
                renames = renames_res_deb)
) %>%
  distinct(year, j0, j5, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(across(any_of(c("j0", "j4", "j42", "j5")), as.character))

# Correction des identifiants j5 pour 1995 à l’aide du fichier de 1996
hh_96 <- read_dta("data/ROS_MDG_microdata/1996/res_deb.dta") %>%
  mutate(j0 = as.character(j0)) %>%
  select(j0, year = NULL, j5_96 = j5, j_1995, j12b) %>%
  filter(j_1995 == 1) %>%
  mutate(year = 1995) %>%
  distinct(j0, j12b, .keep_all = TRUE)

household_locality_all <- household_locality_all %>%
  left_join(hh_96, by = c("j0", "year", "j5" = "j12b")) %>%
  mutate(j5 = ifelse(year == 1995 & !is.na(j5_96), j5_96, j5)) %>%
  select(-j5_96)

# Join with geographical references and add observatory names
household_geolocated <- household_locality_all %>%
  left_join(locality_reference, by = c("j0", "j4", "j42")) %>%
  left_join(observatory_labels, by = c("j0" = "code")) %>%
  relocate(name, .after = j0)
We now have a table where each household is uniquely identified by (year, j5) and linked to its administrative location and observatory label.

title: 4  Variable computation
text:
4.2 Observatory-level segmentation and attrition
Once georeferenced, we segment households by observatory and site. We compute attrition rates, i.e., the share of households that drop out between consecutive survey years. We also identify the modal administrative unit (ADM4) of each site in each year to track potential shifts in the effective coverage of the panel.


Code
# Extract rural observatories and site IDs
household_geolocated <- household_geolocated %>%
  mutate(ro_id = str_sub(j5, 1, 2),
         site_id = str_sub(j5, 1, 3))

# Prepare household-site-year-ADM4 data
hh_site <- household_geolocated %>%
  distinct(ro_id, site_id, j5, year, ADM4_clean)

# Compute household attrition per site_id ---
hh_by_site <- hh_site %>%
  group_by(ro_id, site_id, year) %>%
  summarise(j5_list = list(j5), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(j5_count = map_int(j5_list, length)) %>%
  group_by(ro_id, site_id) %>%
  mutate(previous_year = lag(year)) %>%
  ungroup()

attrition <- hh_by_site %>%
  left_join(hh_by_site %>%
              select(ro_id, site_id, year, 
                     prev_j5 = j5_list, prev_count = j5_count),
            by = c("ro_id", "site_id", "previous_year" = "year")) %>%
  mutate(repeated = map2_int(j5_list, prev_j5, ~length(intersect(.x, .y))),
         attrition_percent = 100 * (prev_count - repeated) / prev_count)

# Compute modal ADM4 per site_id and year ---
modal_adm4 <- hh_site %>%
  filter(!is.na(ADM4_clean)) %>%
  group_by(ro_id, site_id, year, ADM4_clean) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(ro_id, site_id, year) %>%
  mutate(modal_adm4 = ADM4_clean[which.max(n)],
         modal_adm_percent = 100 * max(n) / sum(n)) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(ro_id, site_id, year, modal_adm4, modal_adm_percent)

# Combine everything ---
summary_by_site <- attrition %>%
  select(ro_id, site_id, year, j5_count, attrition_percent) %>%
  left_join(modal_adm4, by = c("ro_id", "site_id", "year"))  %>%
  rename(n = j5_count) %>%
  arrange(ro_id, site_id, year)


The recurrent challenges of ROS data is maintaining longitudinal comparability despite household replacement and site-level redefinitions.

title: 4  Variable computation
text:
4.3 Household composition
We then move to the individual-level files (m* identifiers) to reconstruct household size and demographic profiles. Information on sex (m4), age (m5), and household headship (m6 == 1) is aggregated to build indicators at the household level.


Code
# Load and clean individual data ---------------------------------

# Define variables of interest to extract and standardize
vars_indiv <- c("year", "j0", "j5", "m", "m4", "m5", "m6", "m2a")  

renames_indiv <- list(
  "j0" = c("obsr", "obsr96"),
  "m2a" = c("m2a1", "m2a")  # sera renommée selon l'année
)

years <- 1995:2015

individuals_all_years <- map_dfr(years, function(y) {
  f <- if (y == 1995) "res_m.dta" else "res_m_a.dta"
  
  # Dans certaines années, la variable m2a est absente
  vars_year <- setdiff(vars_indiv, "m2a")  # par défaut, on l’enlève
  renames_year <- renames_indiv
  
  # On ajoute m2a uniquement si elle est disponible
  if (y %in% c(1996, 1997, 2005:2015)) {
    vars_year <- vars_indiv
  }

  load_records(
    year = y,
    file_name = f,
    vars = vars_year,
    renames = renames_year
  ) %>%
    mutate(m2a = if (!"m2a" %in% names(.)) NA_integer_ else m2a)
})
# Count household members -------------------------------------

# Remove duplicates and retain valid members (with age or relationship info)
individuals_cleaned <- individuals_all_years %>%
  distinct(year, j0, j5, m, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  filter(!is.na(m4) | !is.na(m6))

# Count the number of members per household
household_size <- individuals_cleaned %>%
  group_by(year, j0, j5) %>%
  summarise(n_membres = n(), .groups = "drop")

# Check for duplicate household identifiers across observatories
if (sum(duplicated(paste(household_size$year, household_size$j5))) != 0) {
  warning("Certains numéros de ménage sont dupliqués entre observatoires")
} else {
  message("Aucun numéro de ménage dupliqué entre observatoires")
}

# Identify household heads ----------------------------------

# Select individuals who are head of household (m6 == 1)
household_heads_raw <- individuals_cleaned %>%
  filter(m6 == 1, is.na(m2a) | m2a == 1) %>%
  select(year, j0, j5, m, hhh_sex = m4, hhh_age = m5)

# Identify households with more than one head
duplicated_heads <- household_heads_raw %>%
  group_by(year, j5) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n > 1)

# Keep only the first occurrence per household (ordered by member ID)
household_heads_clean <- household_heads_raw %>%
  arrange(year, j5, m) %>%
  distinct(year, j0, j5, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(-m)


We know have a description of the household and hh head demographical characteristics.

title: 4  Variable computation
text:
4.4 Education
Education variables (s1a, s1b, s2, s3a) were not collected consistently across years. For example, reading and writing were not asked in 1996 and 1998, and spurious values appear in some years (e.g., code 0 in 2003). We document these differences, recode consistently, and aggregate to the household level.


Code
# Check education coding across years --------------------

# Define education variables

edu_vars <- c("s1a", "s1b", "s2", "s3a")
years_educ <- setdiff(1995:2015, 1996)

# Function to extract unique values for each variable in a given year
extract_edu_values <- function(year) {
  file_name <- if (year == 1995) "res_m.dta" else "res_m_a.dta"
  file_path <- file.path("data/ROS_MDG_microdata", as.character(year), file_name)
  
  if (!file.exists(file_path)) return(tibble())
  
  df <- read_dta(file_path)
  present_vars <- intersect(edu_vars, names(df))
  
  if (length(present_vars) == 0) return(tibble())
  
  map_dfr(present_vars, function(var) {
    tibble(
      year = year,
      variable = var,
      value = df[[var]] %>% unique() %>% na.omit() %>% as.integer()
    )
  })
}

# Extract all values across years
edu_values_all <- map_dfr(years_educ, extract_edu_values)

# Now: one table per variable, with values as columns and years as rows
edu_presence_tables <- edu_values_all %>%
  mutate(value = as.character(value), present = TRUE) %>%
  group_split(variable) %>%
  map(function(df) {
    df %>%
      select(-variable) %>%
      pivot_wider(
        names_from = value,
        values_from = present,
        values_fill = FALSE
      ) %>%
      arrange(year)
  }) %>%
  set_names(unique(edu_values_all$variable))

Les variables d’éducation sont manquantes pour l’année 1996.J’ai cherché dans le dictionnaire et vérifié les fichiers sources. Après vérification du questionnaire administré en 1996 (dans la documentation), il ressort que ces questions n’ont pas été posées cette année-là (j’imagine qu’on a préféré ne pas reposer la réponse pour les ménages déjà interrogés l’année précédente).
On a donc :

s1a : savez-vous lire ? 1 = oui ; 2 = se débrouille ; 3 = non. Manquant en 1996 et 1998. Valeur 0 présente en 2003 (pas présente dans le questionnaire).
s1b savez-vous écrire ? 1 = oui ; 2 = se débrouille ; 3 = non. Manquant en 1996 et 1998. Valeur 0 présente en 2003 (pas présente dans le questionnaire).
s2 : avez-vous été ou allez-vous à l’école primaire. 1 = oui, 2 = non. Manquant en 1996.
s3a : nombre d’années d’études. Manquant en 1996.

On extrait et on recode donc ces variables en fonction de ces informations.


Code
# Define education variables and identifiers
vars_educ <- c("year", "j0", "j5", "m", "s1a", "s1b", "s2", "s3a")

# Rename j0 if needed
renames_educ <- list("j0" = c("obsr", "obsr96"))

# 3. Define years to include (excluding 1996)
years_educ <- setdiff(1995:2015, 1996)

# 4. Load education data across years
education_all_years <- map_dfr(years_educ, function(y) {
  f <- if (y == 1995) "res_m.dta" else "res_m_a.dta"
  load_records(y, file_name = f, vars = vars_educ, renames = renames_educ)
})

# clean and recode
education_cleaned <- education_all_years %>%
  mutate(
    # delete variables not defined in the questionnaire (in 2003 only)
    s1a = na_if(s1a, 0),
    s1b = na_if(s1b, 0),
    
    # recode reading/writing variables
    s1a_cat = case_when(
      s1a == 1 ~ "oui",
      s1a == 2 ~ "se débrouille",
      s1a == 3 ~ "non",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    s1b_cat = case_when(
      s1b == 1 ~ "oui",
      s1b == 2 ~ "se débrouille",
      s1b == 3 ~ "non",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    
    # recode schooling variable
    s2_bin = case_when(
      s2 == 1 ~ TRUE,
      s2 == 2 ~ FALSE,
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_
    ),
    
    # s3a est conservé tel quel (nombre d'années d'étude)
    s3a = na_if(s3a, 0)  # 0 n'est pas une valeur valide
  ) %>%
  distinct(year, j0, j5, m, .keep_all = TRUE)
  

# join with individual data
individuals_with_education <- individuals_cleaned %>%
  left_join(
    education_cleaned %>%
      select(year, j0, j5, m, s1a_cat, s1b_cat, s2_bin, s3a),
    by = c("year", "j0", "j5", "m")
  )

education_household_summary <- individuals_with_education %>%
  group_by(year, j0, j5) %>%
  summarise(
    # Presence of any literate adult (age ≥ 15 and reads "oui")
    any_literate_adult = any(s1a_cat == "oui" & m5 >= 15, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # Highest education in household (max years)
    max_years_edu = max(s3a, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # Mean years of education (all members)
    mean_years_edu = mean(s3a, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # Share of members with any schooling (age ≥ 6 and s2_bin == TRUE)
    pct_with_schooling = mean(s2_bin[m5 >= 6], na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # Presence of adult who can read
    any_adult_can_read = any(s1a_cat %in% c("oui", "se débrouille") & m5 >= 15, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # Average years of education among adults (age ≥ 15)
    mean_years_edu_adults = mean(s3a[m5 >= 15], na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # Education variables for household head
    hhh_s1a = first(s1a_cat[m6 == 1]),
    hhh_s1b = first(s1b_cat[m6 == 1]),
    hhh_s2 = first(s2_bin[m6 == 1]),
    hhh_s3a = first(s3a[m6 == 1])
  ) %>%
  ungroup()


Nous avons donc construit un jeu additionnel education_household_summary avec plusieurs indicateurs synthétiques au niveau du ménage à partir des informations individuelles sur l’éducation. Ces indicateurs incluent :

la présence d’au moins un adulte sachant lire (any_literate_adult), défini comme ayant répondu “oui” à la question sur la lecture (s1a_cat) et ayant 15 ans ou plus,
la présence d’au moins un adulte pouvant lire, qu’il sache lire ou “se débrouille” (any_reading_adult),
le nombre d’années d’éducation le plus élevé observé dans le ménage (max_years_schooling),
le nombre moyen d’années d’éducation parmi les membres du ménage (mean_years_schooling),
la proportion de membres âgés de 6 ans ou plus ayant déjà été ou allant à l’école (share_with_any_schooling),
ainsi que le nombre moyen d’années d’éducation parmi les adultes de 15 ans ou plus (mean_years_schooling_adult).

Par ailleurs, nous extrayons pour chaque ménage les quatre variables d’éducation relatives au chef de ménage : sa capacité à lire (hhh_s1a_cat), à écrire (hhh_s1b_cat), sa déclaration de fréquentation de l’école (hhh_s2_bin) et le nombre d’années d’éducation déclarées (hhh_s3a).

title: 4  Variable computation
text:
4.5 Agricultural activities
A key dimension of household livelihoods is the degree of engagement in agriculture and related activities. To capture this, we exploit the individual activity codes (a1) recorded for each household member. Before using these variables, it is necessary to verify the consistency of activity codes across survey years.
We begin by extracting the list of activity codes from each year (1996–2015) and checking whether their labels remained stable over time.


Code
extract_a1_labels <- function(year) {
  file_path <- file.path("data/ROS_MDG_microdata", as.character(year), 
                         "res_m_a.dta")
 read_dta(file_path) %>%
    select(code = a1) %>%
    unique() %>%
    mutate(year = year,
           label = to_character(code))
}

# Appliquer aux années disponibles
years <- 1996:2015
a1_labels_all_years <- map_dfr(years, extract_a1_labels)

# Pivot large : lignes = codes, colonnes = années, cellules = libellés
a1_labels_table <- a1_labels_all_years %>%
  mutate(label = as.character(label)) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = label,
    values_fill = list(label = "-")
  ) %>%
  arrange(code)


We then extract individual activity information for all available years. For most surveys (1996–2015), the variable a1 directly identifies the main activity of each individual.


Code
# Années pour lesquelles on dispose des activités individuelles
years_activ_indiv <- 1996:2015

# Définir les variables à extraire
vars_activ_indiv <- c("year", "j0", "j5", "m", "a1")
renames_vars_activ_indiv <- list("j0" = "obsr96")
# Charger les données avec load_records
activ_indiv_all_years <- map_dfr(years_activ_indiv, function(x) {
  load_records(
    year = x,
    file_name = "res_m_a.dta",
    vars = vars_activ_indiv,
    renames = renames_vars_activ_indiv
  )
})


The 1995 survey did not follow the same format. Instead of asking each individual for their main activity, the questionnaires identified the household’s main and secondary activities, as well as which members were involved. We therefore reconstruct individual activities from two separate files (res_apm.dta and res_asm.dta), prioritizing main activities when both are available.


Code
# Charger les deux fichiers de 1995
apm_1995 <- read_dta("data/ROS_MDG_microdata/1995/res_apm.dta")
asm_1995 <- read_dta("data/ROS_MDG_microdata/1995/res_asm.dta")

# Nettoyage de l'activité principale du ménage (res_apm)
activ_1995_main <- apm_1995 %>%
  transmute(
    year = 1995,
    j5 = j5,
    m = as.integer(apm12a),
    a1 = as.numeric(apm11),
    source = "main"
  )

# Nettoyage de l'activité secondaire du ménage (res_asm)
activ_1995_secondary <- asm_1995 %>%
  transmute(
    year = 1995,
    j5 = j5,
    m = as.integer(asm31),
    a1 = as.numeric(asm32),
    source = "secondary"
  )

# Combiner les deux et ne garder qu'une ligne par individu
activ_1995_unique <- bind_rows(activ_1995_main, activ_1995_secondary) %>%
  arrange(j5, m, desc(source)) %>%  # priorité à "main"
  distinct(j5, m, .keep_all = TRUE)  # on garde la première occurrence

# Fusion avec les autres années
activ_indiv_all_years <- bind_rows(activ_indiv_all_years, activ_1995_unique %>% 
                                     select(-source))


Once the individual-level activity table is harmonized, we aggregate it at the household–year level. We distinguish between two levels of agricultural engagement:

Stricto sensu agriculture (agro_stricto): farming or livestock rearing, coded as 95 and 96.
Lato sensu agriculture (agro_lato): a broader set of codes encompassing farming, livestock, fishing, gathering, apiculture, and agriculture-related crafts.



Code
# Codes d'activité pour les regroupements
codes_agro_stricto <- c(95, 96)
codes_agro_lato <- c(4, 5, 6, 13, 20, 21, 24, 25, 32, 59, 70, 76, 85, 95, 96, 
                     97, 98, 99)

# Agrégation par ménage et année
activ_menage_annee <- activ_indiv_all_years %>%
  mutate(
    is_agro_stricto = a1 %in% codes_agro_stricto,
    is_agro_lato = a1 %in% codes_agro_lato
  ) %>%
  group_by(year, j5) %>%
  summarise(
    hhh_activ = {
      chef_vals <- a1[which(m == 1)]
      if (length(chef_vals) > 0) chef_vals[1] else NA_real_
    },
    hhh_activ_agro_stricto = hhh_activ %in% codes_agro_stricto,
    hhh_activ_agro_lato = hhh_activ %in% codes_agro_lato,
    hh_any_agro_stricto = any(is_agro_stricto, na.rm = TRUE),
    hh_any_agro_lato = any(is_agro_lato, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


The resulting table activ_menage_annee includes several household-level indicators:

hhh_activ: the main activity of the household head,
hhh_activ_agro_stricto: whether the household head is strictly engaged in farming or livestock,
hhh_activ_agro_lato: whether the household head is engaged in agriculture more broadly,
hh_any_agro_stricto: whether at least one member of the household is strictly engaged in farming or livestock,=
hh_any_agro_lato: whether at least one member of the household is broadly engaged in agricultural or related activities.

This classification makes it possible to characterize households according to their insertion in the agricultural sector, capturing both specialization (stricto sensu) and diversification into related activities (lato sensu).

title: 4  Variable computation
text:
4.6 Food security
Food security questions were phrased differently across years, but one consistent element is the number of months of self-sufficiency from household production. We harmonize all available questions into a single measure, food_selfsuff_months, capped at 12 months.
Les questions relatives à la sécurité alimentaire ont beaucoup varié d’une année à l’autre dans les enquêtes ROS. Néanmoins, une question reste globalement comparable : la durée (en mois) pendant laquelle la production vivrière du ménage suffit à couvrir ses besoins alimentaires. Selon les années, cette information est captée de manière légèrement différente :

1995 (sa3a) : “Combien de mois votre production en aliment de base vous suffit-il ?”
1996–1997 (sa2) : “Combien de mois de l’année votre production en aliment de base vous suffit ?”
1998–2015 (sa2a, sa2b, sa2c) : Nombre de mois d’autosuffisance en riz (1ère et 2ème saison) et en maïs.

Nous agrégeons ici toutes ces variables dans une seule mesure standardisée : food_selfsuff_months, plafonnée à 12 mois.


Code
sa_95 <- load_records(
  year = 1995,
  file_name = "res_sa2.dta",
  vars = c("year", "j5", "food_selfsuff_months"),
  renames = c("food_selfsuff_months" = "sa3a")
  ) %>%
  mutate(source_food_selfsuff = "sa3a") 

sa_9697 <- map_dfr(1996:1997, ~load_records(
  year = .x,
  file_name = "res_sa2.dta",
  vars = c("year", "j5", "food_selfsuff_months"),
  renames = list("food_selfsuff_months" = "sa2")
) %>%
  mutate(
    source_food_selfsuff = "sa2"
  ) 
)

sa_9814 <- map(1998:2014, ~load_records(
  year = .x,
  file_name = "res_sa2.dta",
  vars = c("year", "j5", "sa2a", "sa2b", "sa2c")
)) %>%
  map(~.x %>%
  mutate(
    sa2a = as.numeric(sa2a),
    sa2b = as.numeric(sa2b),
    sa2c = as.numeric(sa2c)
  )
) %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(
    food_selfsuff_months = rowSums(across(c(sa2a, sa2b, sa2c)), na.rm = TRUE),
    source_food_selfsuff = "sa2a+sa2b+sa2c"
  ) %>%
  select(year, j5, food_selfsuff_months, source_food_selfsuff)

sa_15 <- load_records(
  year = 2015,
  file_name = "res_sa2_2015.dta",
  vars = c("year", "j5", "sa2a", "sa2b", "sa2c")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    food_selfsuff_months = rowSums(across(c(sa2a, sa2b, sa2c)), na.rm = TRUE),
    source_food_selfsuff = "sa2a+sa2b+sa2c"
  ) %>%
  select(year, j5, food_selfsuff_months, source_food_selfsuff)

# Bind and cap to 12 months
sa_all <- bind_rows(sa_95, sa_9697, sa_9814, sa_15) %>%
  mutate(food_selfsuff_months = pmin(food_selfsuff_months, 12))


Lorsque plusieurs cultures sont prises en compte (riz 1ère saison, 2ème saison, maïs), nous additionnons les mois d’autosuffisance déclarés, tout en plafonnant la somme à 12 mois pour éviter les surestimations. La variable source_food_selfsuff permet de tracer l’origine des données selon l’année.

title: 4  Variable computation
text:
4.7 Incomes
We reconstructed the various components of rural Malagasy household income based on ROS surveys (1995–2015), reproducing the processing carried out in Stata in for the latest surveys. The aim aim to produce a total income that is consistent and comparable over time, taking into account the specific characteristics of each survey wave. The main difficulty lies in the heterogeneity of the questionnaires and data structures between years: changing variable names, divergent formats, and the absence or presence of specific modules.


Code
# Chargement des fonctions
source("Calc_revenus_all_years.R")

# Chargement + nettoyage immédiat
revenus <- compute_income_all_years()


The reference script Calc_revenus_all_years.R contains a suite of functions, each dedicated to one component of income:

revppal: income from the main activity,
revsec: income from secondary activities,
rev_riz: net rice income (production minus charges),
rev_cu: net income from other crops,
revel: livestock income,
revpeche: fishing income (2015 only),
rente_riz, rente_cu: land rents,
autre_rev: miscellaneous incomes,
himo: high labor intensity public works (HIMO),
decap: exceptional sales (land, cattle, equipment, durables),
transrecmo and transrecnomo: transfers (monetary and non-monetary).

These functions rely on harmonized household identifiers and systematically handle missing files, variable name changes, and differences in questionnaire design. They make it possible to reconstruct three aggregate measures:

Current income (revcou) = revppal + revsec + rev_riz + rev_cu + revel + revpeche
Exceptional income (revexcept) = rente_riz + rente_cu + autre_rev + himo + decap + vte_biens + transrecmo + transrecnomo
Total income (revtot) = revcou + revexcept

title: 4  Variable computation
text:
4.8 Consolidation
Finally, we merge all household-level variables — demographic, educational, food security, and income — into a single consolidated dataset. We ensure that (year, j5) is unique, check for potential duplications, and save the result for further analysis.


Code
# Harmonisation des identifiants dans les autres tables

# Une fonction pour forcer l'unicité j5 + year
clean_all_components <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    mutate(j5 = as.character(j5), year = as.integer(year)) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.logical), as.numeric)) %>% 
    group_by(year, j5) %>%
    summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop")
}

revenus_clean <- clean_all_components(revenus) 
household_size <- clean_all_components(household_size)
household_heads_clean <- clean_all_components(household_heads_clean)
education_household_summary <- clean_all_components(education_household_summary)
activ_menage_annee <- clean_all_components(activ_menage_annee) 
sa_all <- clean_all_components(sa_all) 
revenus <- clean_all_components(revenus) 
household_geolocated <- clean_all_components(household_geolocated) 

# Étape 2 – Fusion avec les autres sources de données
household_consolidated <- household_geolocated %>%
  left_join(household_size, by = c("year", "j5")) %>%
  left_join(household_heads_clean, by = c("year", "j5")) %>%
  left_join(education_household_summary, by = c("year", "j5")) %>%
  left_join(activ_menage_annee, by = c("year", "j5")) %>%
  left_join(sa_all, by = c("year", "j5")) %>%
  left_join(revenus_clean, by = c("year", "j5"))

# Étape 3 – Vérification d’unicité
dup_check <- household_consolidated %>%
  count(year, j5) %>%
  filter(n > 1)

if (nrow(dup_check) == 0) {
  message("Acune duplication détectée : l'identifiant (year, j5) est unique.")
} else {
  warning("Duplication détectée pour certains couples (year, j5). Vérifiez les sources.")
  print(dup_check)
}

write_rds(household_consolidated, "data/household_consolidated.rds")


This dataset forms the backbone of our study, allowing us to assess the relationship between conservation policies and household living conditions in a harmonized longitudinal perspective.

title: 5  Marovoay-Ankarafantsika
text:
5.1 Protected area expansion
The Marovoay rural observatory offers an outstanding opportunities to study the socio-economic impacts of protected areas in Madagascar. This is because its panel data coincides both spatially and temporally with the expansion of Ankarafantsika, one of the country’s oldest and most emblematic protected areas. By comparing villages located on different sides of the Betsiboka river, we can build a quasi-experimental design to estimate how the 2002 reclassification of the reserve into a national park affected local households.

title: 5  Marovoay-Ankarafantsika
text:
5.1.1 Ankarafantsika before 2002
Ankarafantsika was first created as a Réserve Naturelle Intégrale (RNI) in 1927, with boundaries covering only a fraction of today’s surface:

Septième réserve naturelle. — Plateau d’Ankarafantsika, situé dans le district de Marovoay, région de Majunga, superficie approximative : 66.541 hectares, ayant pour limites: Au nord, la propriété dite: « Sainte-Marie Marovoay », titre n° 784-M,dts terrains domaniaux et, à une distance de cinq kilomètres environ, les villages d’Ampombomangarakaraka et Beronono ; A l’est, des terrains domaniaux; Au sud, des terrains dumaniaux et, à quelque distance, des villages d’Ankorika et de Bevasaka ; A l’ouest, des terrains domaniaux et la rivière Mahajamba. Tel au surplus que cette réserve naturelle est figurée à l’un des trois plans annexés audit arrêté. Décret du 31 décembre 1927

Over the decades, its legal status evolved through a series of decrees and classifications:

la Réserve Naturelle Intégrale d’Ankarafantsika fut créée en 1927 et ses limites ont été précisées en 1966 avec le Décret n° 66-242 du 1 juin 1966 (60 520 ha). Parallèlement, des territoires de la Forêt d’Ankarafantsika sur les districts de Marovoay et Ambato Boeny ont été classés réserves forestières avec l’Arrêté du 24 décembre 1929 (75 000 ha). De plus, le Jardin botanique d’Ampijoroa (district d’Ambato Boeny, 91 ha), recensé en 1969 par le Domaine Forestier National est devenu la Station Forestière d’Ampijoroa (4974 ha) en 1999 par l’Arrêté interministériel n° 13-056/99 du 7 décembre 1999. En 2002, la réserve naturelle intégrale créée en 1927 et reclassée en 1966, les réserves forestières instituées en 1929 ainsi que la Station Forestière d’Ampijoroa sont toutes instituées en un seul parc national (Décret n° 2002-798 du 7 août 2002, 130 000 ha). Ce dernier subit un changement de limites en 2015 sous le Décret n° 2015-730 du 21 avril 2015 ; Dernière modification de statut : suivant le Décret n° 2015-730 du 21 avril 2015 ; Surface actuelle : 136 513 ha (selon le décret en vigueur). (Goodman et al. 2018, vol. 2, p. 157)”

The extension of the protected area in 2002 was mapped as follows in 2002 by experts from the NGO Conservation International, which spearheaded the initiative.
 The objective of this study is to assess the impact of the 2002 expansion on the populations of villages that became adjacent to the RNI at that time.
Some details on the status of the forest reserve that was transformed into an RNI during the expansion:

Par arrêté du Gouverneur Général p. i., en date du 24 décembre 1929, pris en conseil d’administration, est mise en réserve, dans les conditions fixées par les articles 50 à 52 du décret du 28 août 1913, la portion du massif forestier dit de l’Ankarafantsika, situé à l’ouest de la 7e réserve naturelle créée par le décret du 31 décembre 1927, dans la province de Marovoay ; La réserve ainsi instituée, d’une surface approximative de 75.000 hectares telle qu’elle est figurée au plan ci-annexé, est limitée: Au nord, par une ligne droite partant de l’angle N. W. de la 7e réserve naturelle et allant jusqu’au village d’Ampombilavakely, puis de ce village jusqu’à la limite de la propriété dite « Croix Rousse » titre n°3153; A l’ouest, par les propriété dites « Croix Rousse et Mont-rouge » titre no 3153 — M. et 2970 — M jusqu’au vilhge de Bongomaro ; Au sud, par la concession n°1059, jusqu’au nord du village de Beilalana, puis; par une ligne droite passant par le village de Bedo et allant jusqu’à l’angle S. W. de la 7e réserve naturelle ; A l’est, par la 7e réserve naturelle.

Articles 50 to 52 of the 1913 Forest Code refer to the forest reserve regime. However, there is little information on what this entails in terms of rules. More importantly, subsequent analysis reveal that there was no effective control over the forest reserve (Brondeau 1999).

title: 5  Marovoay-Ankarafantsika
text:
5.2 Survey sites location
The Marovoay observatory conducted panel household surveys nearly continuously from 1995 to 2014 (with an interruption in 2009 due to the national political crisis). To analyze treatment effects, we need to identify which survey sites are located inside or near the expanded protected area.


Code
library(tidyverse) # A series of packages for data manipulation
library(haven) # Required for reading STATA files (.dta)
library(labelled) # To work with labelled data from STATA
library(sf) # for spatial data handling
library(stringdist) # for string distance and matching
library(tmap) # for mapping
library(fuzzyjoin) # for fuzzy joining
library(readxl) # Read data frames to Excel format
library(writexl) # Write data frames to Excel format
library(gt)  # for nicely formatted tables
library(wdpar)
library(panelView)
# remotes::install_github("https://github.com/xuyiqing/gsynth")
library(gsynth)
library(purrr)



observatory_names <- read_xlsx("data/observatory_names.xlsx")

obs_maro <- read_rds("output/correspondence_table4.rds") %>% 
  mutate(j0 = as.numeric(j0)) %>%
  left_join(observatory_names, by = c("j0" = "code")) %>%
  rename(OBS_NAME = name) %>%
  relocate(OBS_NAME, .before = j0) %>%
  filter(OBS_NAME == "Marovoay")

obs_maro_communes <- st_read(
  "data/Observatoires_ROS_communes_COD_v3.gpkg",
  quiet = TRUE) %>%
  left_join(select(observatory_names, name, code), 
            by = c("OBS_NAME" = "name")) %>%
  rename(OBS_CODE = code) %>%
  filter(OBS_NAME == "Marovoay")

obs_maro_fokontany <- st_read(
  "data/OCHA_BNGRC admin boundaries/mdg_admbnda_adm4_BNGRC_OCHA_20181031.shp",
  quiet = TRUE) %>%
  filter(ADM3_PCODE %in% obs_maro_communes$ADM3_PCODE & !is.na(OBS_NAME))

ankarafantsika_2025 <- wdpa_read("data/WDPA_WDOECM_Jul2025_Public_MDG.zip") %>% 
  filter(NAME == "Ankarafantsika")

tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(obs_maro_fokontany %>% 
           filter(ADM4_EN %in% c("Maroala", "Ampijoroa"))) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "lightblue", col = "darkblue",
              fill.legend = tm_legend_hide()) +
  tm_text(text = "ADM4_EN", fontface = "bold", ymod = 3, xmod = -3) + 
  tm_shape(obs_maro_fokontany %>% 
             filter(ADM4_EN %in% c("Bepako", "Madiromiongana"))) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "lightgreen", col = "darkgreen",
              fill.legend = tm_legend_hide()) +
  tm_text(text = "ADM4_EN", fontface = "bold", ymod = 3, xmod = -3) + 
  tm_shape(ankarafantsika_2025) +
  tm_borders(col = "darkgreen") +
  tm_fill(fill = "darkgreen", fill_alpha = 0.3) + 
  tm_text(text = "NAME") +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_basemap("Esri.WorldGrayCanvas")






This map shows the four relevant sites: Bepako and Madiromiongana, located on the same side of the Betsiboka river as Ankarafantsika, and Ampijoroa and Maroala, located across the river.
Although the latter two appear geographically close “as the crow flies,” in practice the Betsiboka forms a major natural barrier. Crossing is possible only under certain hydrological conditions, often requiring long detours or costly boat transport. In practice, flows of people, goods, and services are much denser along the Marovoay downstream axis than across the river. This physical separation strengthens the plausibility of using the cross-river sites as a control group.

title: 5  Marovoay-Ankarafantsika
text:
5.3 Available observations

5.3.1 Marovoay observatory only
To proceed with the evaluation, we document the size of the household panels in each site and year, and assign treatment status. The treatment definition follows the 2002 expansion: households in Bepako and Madiromiongana are coded as “treated” (pre-2002 vs. post-2002), while Ampijoroa and Maroala serve as untreated controls.


Code
# Load the locality correspondence table with administrative codes
locality_reference <- readr::read_rds("output/correspondence_table5.rds") %>% 
  select(j0, j42, j4, ADM3_PCODE, ADM3_EN, ADM4_PCODE, ADM4_clean)

# Load observatory names and match them to their codes
observatory_labels <- read_xlsx("data/observatory_names.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(code = as.character(code)) %>%
  select(code, name)

# Function to rename variables using a named list
# e.g. renames = list("j0" = c("obsr", "obsr96"))
rename_all_custom <- function(df, renames) {
  if (length(renames) == 0) return(df)
  for (new_name in names(renames)) {
    # Skip renaming if new_name already exists in df
    if (new_name %in% names(df)) next
    old_names <- renames[[new_name]]
    matched_old <- old_names[old_names %in% names(df)]
    if (length(matched_old) > 0) {
      df <- df %>% rename(!!new_name := all_of(matched_old[1]))
    }
  }
  return(df)
}

# Generic function to load and standardize records from any year
# Arguments:
#   - year: numeric year of the survey
#   - vars: vector of variables to select (after renaming)
#   - renames: named list of renaming rules (new_name = c(possible_old_names))
load_records <- function(year, file_name, vars, renames = list()) {
  path <- paste0("data/ROS_MDG_microdata/", year, "/")
  df <- read_dta(paste0(path, file_name))

  df <- rename_all_custom(df, renames)

  # Ensure all expected vars exist (fill missing with NA)
  missing_vars <- setdiff(vars, names(df))
  df[missing_vars] <- NA

  # Handle j0 if not in original file
  if (!"j0" %in% names(df)) {
    df <- df %>%
      mutate(j0 = substr(j5, 1, 2)) %>% 
      mutate(j0 = as.character(as.numeric(j0)))
  }

  df %>%
    mutate(j0 = as.character(as.numeric(j0))) %>%
    select(any_of(vars))
}

The resulting heatmap presents three key insights:

Early years (1995–1997): only the two treated sites (same side of the river) were included in the survey. This means that the earliest baseline lacks control villages, which will lead to discard these years from comparisons.
Post-1998: the two control sites were added, creating a four-site structure that enables a difference-in-differences design.
Attrition and coverage: while household counts vary across years, the overall panel remains sufficiently populated to support longitudinal analysis.



5.3.2 Larger control pool
While the Marovoay observatory offers a natural treated–control comparison across the Betsiboka river, restricting the control group to its two sites limits statistical power. We therefore enlarge the control pool to include all other ROS sites that have both pre- and post-2002 observations. This approach relies on the same identification strategy — comparing households adjacent to the expanded Ankarafantsika park to those in unaffected areas — but increases sample size and improves the precision of estimates.

title: 5  Marovoay-Ankarafantsika
text:
5.4 Results (provisional and subject to change)






Important



Note that this is very rough result at this stage. We need to refine the variable calculation, perform outlier identification, carefully reconsider the choice of outcome variables (on education and food security), strenghten model specification and conduct robustness checks.


The figures plot event-study coefficients relative to the year of expansion, while tables report average treatment effects on the treated (ATT).
The synthetic control estimations do not show systematic evidence of income gains for households living adjacent to Ankarafantsika following the 2002 PA extension. For total income (revtot) and constructed income (revcou), the average treatment effects are negative, though not statistically significant, with confidence intervals spanning both positive and negative values. The time profiles suggest some short-term increases around the mid-2000s, followed by a decline, but the uncertainty margins remain wide.
Disaggregating by income source points to a similar pattern. Agricultural revenues (rev_agri_current) display negative average effects, while non-agricultural revenues (rev_nonagri_current) show no consistent trend, with only a brief positive deviation in the mid-2000s. Taken together, these results suggest that households did not experience sustained income growth as a result of the park expansion, and if anything, agricultural activities may have been more adversely affected.
The composition of household activities also does not show discernible shifts. Neither the share of agriculture in total income nor the probability that the household head is an agricultural worker register significant changes, and the share of household members in agro-related activities remains flat. This indicates that diversification away from agriculture was not triggered by the protected area expansion.
Broader welfare indicators lead to similar conclusions. Food self-sufficiency months show no significant improvement; if anything, point estimates turn negative towards the later years, though again with large confidence intervals. Similarly, youth schooling rates remain unaffected throughout the observation window .

text:
5.5 (very preliminary) Discussion
At this stage, the first raw estimates point to no robust positive socio-economic impacts on local households. The evidence is more consistent with a neutral or slightly negative effect, particularly in agricultural income, though with considerable statistical uncertainty.
